The Jacobins. The most powerful radical faction within the French Revolution, named after their meeting place in a former monastery—the Jacobin convent. The Jacobin Club evolved from a salon of moderate revolutionaries into a formidable political organization whose members, including Robespierre, Danton, and Marat, dominated the revolutionary government during the Reign of Terror. Their pursuit of republican ideals and revolutionary justice fundamentally shaped the Revolution's trajectory and legacy. The Jacobins originated as the Society of Friends of the Constitution in seventeen eighty-nine, meeting in the Jacobin convent in Paris to discuss revolutionary principles and debate how to implement the Revolution. The convent location gave them their enduring name. The organization grew into a nationwide network of clubs promoting revolutionary ideology, with over two thousand affiliated societies by seventeen ninety-three—a powerful organizing structure that spread radical ideas throughout France and coordinated political action. The Jacobins embodied radical revolutionary principles: republicanism against any return to monarchy, popular sovereignty with power derived from the people, and economic equality. They were far more radical than the moderate Girondins, who sought constitutional monarchy or limited republic. The Jacobins dominated the radical phase of the Revolution from seventeen ninety-two to seventeen ninety-four. They controlled the Committee of Public Safety, the executive body, and drove the Reign of Terror—a period of systematic executions targeting perceived enemies of the Revolution. They advocated for the execution of King Louis XVI, which happened in seventeen ninety-three, the abolition of feudalism and the church, de-Christianization of France, and aggressive defense of the Revolution against internal counter-revolutionary plots and external invasion by monarchical powers. Under Robespierre's leadership, they transformed into the instrument of Revolutionary Terror. They implemented mass executions—over forty thousand died, though many executions were local—virtue-centered ideology, and suppression of perceived counter-revolutionary activity, religious practice, and even rival revolutionary factions. The Jacobins collapsed with Robespierre's execution in July seventeen ninety-four, the Thermidor reaction, ending the Terror and ushering in the more conservative Directory. Jacobin power was broken, many surviving Jacobins were executed or imprisoned, and the Revolution's radical phase ended.
